quiz.q: Which Anypoint Platform module is used in the Design step of the API lifecycle?
quiz.explain: APIs are designed in Design Center with RAML; Runtime Manager deploys, API Manager secures and Anypoint Monitoring monitors.

quiz.q: You need to start, stop or restart a deployed Mule application and check its logs. Which tool do you use?
quiz.explain: Runtime Manager handles deployment (CloudHub or on-premises) and lets you start/stop/restart apps and view logs.

quiz.q: What is the output of the Design step called?
quiz.explain: Design produces the API specification, which defines requests, responses, errors, security and resource paths, usually in RAML.

quiz.q: Why must MuleSoft developers know Postman even though QA does detailed testing?
options: It is the only way to view Mule logs
It acts as the front-end so you can test the API without waiting for the front-end team
It is required to deploy apps to CloudHub
quiz.explain: If the React/JS front-end isn't ready, Postman sends requests to the API and checks responses.

quiz.q: According to the instructor, what is the biggest disadvantage of point-to-point integration?
options: It requires a vCore licence per system
A change in one system forces changes in every integration connected to it
quiz.explain: If 50 systems are integrated with one system and it changes, all 50 integrations may need changes. Adding systems also multiplies integrations.

quiz.q: Which three features make MuleSoft an ESB tool?
quiz.explain: These are the defining ESB features on the slide; enrichment is a part of transformation.

quiz.q: A small bug fix in password reset is needed in a monolithic banking app. What happens?
options: The whole application is redeployed, and all services (login, balance check, fund transfer) are down during it
Only the password-reset service is redeployed
The fix is applied without any downtime
quiz.explain: In a monolith every feature is packaged as one app, so any change means full redeployment and downtime for everything.

quiz.q: In festive season only 20 of 100 services receive extra traffic. What advantage do microservices give here?
options: Resources can be increased only for those 20 services
All 100 services are scaled together automatically
No extra servers are ever needed
quiz.explain: Targeted scalability: a monolith must scale the whole app, wasting resources. Auto-scaling is a premium, extra-cost feature.

quiz.q: Why do microservices increase MuleSoft cost?
options: Licensing is based on vCores, and more applications need more vCores
Each microservice needs its own Anypoint Platform account
Each microservice requires a DR site
quiz.explain: A vCore is a unit of CPU and memory; more applications consume more vCores and raise cost.

quiz.q: Which API-led layer contains the business logic — which systems to call, in what order, and how to shape the response?
quiz.explain: The Process API orchestrates and transforms. System APIs only connect to one back-end; Experience APIs are exposed to the front-end.

quiz.q: Shipment status comes from one system and the System API response is already in the right shape. What may the architect do?
options: Let the Experience API call the System API directly, skipping the Process API
Make the front-end call the database directly
Convert the System API into a monolith
quiz.explain: API-led connectivity is a best practice, not mandatory; skipping an unneeded Process API saves resources.

quiz.q: A System API's internal connection logic changes but its response structure stays the same. What must change in the Process and Experience APIs?
quiz.explain: Internal changes don't ripple. Only if the response structure (contract) changes must consuming APIs be updated.

cards.back: Design (Design Center) → Implementation (Anypoint Studio) → Deploy (Runtime Manager) → Test (QA, Postman) → Secure (API Manager) → Monitor (Anypoint Monitoring).
The design document of an API (also API spec / API contract): resources, requests, success and error responses, examples, schemas, security. Written in RAML or OAS.
RAML = RESTful API Modeling Language; OAS = OpenAPI Specification, an alternative. Almost all MuleSoft projects use RAML.
The IDE where Mule applications are implemented — connectors, components, DataWeave — and run locally for testing.
Deploys apps (CloudHub or on-premises); start, stop, restart; view logs and basic statistics.
Anypoint Platform module used to secure APIs with policies.
Functional: Postman, SoapUI. Performance (pre-prod, by separate testers): JMeter, LoadRunner.
Direct integration between each pair of systems. New systems add many links, and a change in one system ripples to all connected integrations.
Enterprise Service Bus — a central architecture all systems connect to once. MuleSoft is an ESB tool ("Mule ESB developer" = MuleSoft developer).
Coordinating calls to systems in the right sequence — like a music conductor (check stock → payment → bill → delivery).
Converting data between formats/structures, e.g. JSON from the mobile app → XML for SAP. Written in DataWeave.
A part of transformation that enhances data: first + last name → full name; date of birth → age.
All business services in one application. Simple at first, but complexity and response time grow, any change means full redeploy, and if it's down everything is down.
Each meaningful business service is a separate application — less complexity, reusable, independently scalable, reliable.
More resources and vCore cost, inter-service communication over the network, and contract changes affect all consumers.

cards.front: Who decides how to split services?
cards.back: The solution architect, not the developer. Hybrids (2–3 related services in one app) are common.
MuleSoft's licensing/sizing unit of CPU and memory. More applications → more vCores → higher cost.
A premium MuleSoft feature at extra cost. Without it, resources are raised manually before known events like sale days.
MuleSoft's best-practice (not mandatory) strategy: reusable, purposeful APIs in three layers — Experience, Process, System.
Exposed to the front-end; reshapes data so the intended audience (mobile, web) can consume it easily.
Holds business logic; consumes System APIs (and possibly other Process APIs) and shapes data per requirement.
Connects to one back-end system and gets/sends data, with no business logic. Usually one per system.

cards.front: Why separate Experience APIs for mobile and web?
cards.back: They may need different amounts of data, response structures or security; Process and System APIs are reused.

cards.front: Upstream vs. downstream (for a System API)
cards.back: Upstream = the Process/Experience APIs above it that call it; downstream = the back-end system below it.
Yes — especially in regulated industries like banks audited by the RBI. "It's internal" is not a reason to skip it.
